extracted.intended_audience: general newspaper readers (WWII-era news consumers) and researchers of historical press coverage
extracted.subtask_description: Contemporaneous Associated Press news dispatches and front‑page stories covering wartime events, politics, human-interest accounts, official statements and survival/recommendations intended for general readers. Includes datelines, agency attribution, named officials, eyewitness quotes, and practical guidance from experts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lifeboat provisions and survival measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommendations for what lifeboats and survivors should have and do (as reported by a Navy doctor and survivors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Could furnish an adequate diet for torpedo victims with a shotgun, spear and fishing gear; stock lifeboats with heavy oil; include tablets of brewer’s yeast to provide an ample supply of vitamin B complex; circulate legs and feet by removing tight shoes, flexing toes, stretching legs and swimming alongside the lifeboat; grease skin to protect against salt-water blisters and cold; survivors should be carried aboard rescue ships because walking may permanently injure or infect damaged skin tissue. (All guidance is presented in the article under the heading 'Lifeboats Should Carry, Guns, Fishing Gear, Navy Doctor Says'.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Dateline and agency attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of a city dateline with date and explicit agency credit (e.g., 'WASHINGTON; March 5' and '(A. P.)' or 'By the Associated Press').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each dispatch is labeled with a dateline and the Associated Press credit, signaling origin and timeliness of report. Datelines anchor stories in place/time and agency credit establishes source responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Named sourcing and direct quotations
rubrics_metrics.description: Identification of named officials, survivors and experts with direct quoted material (e.g., Senator Guffey, Representative Lambertson, Elmer Davis, Capt. Lorence, survivors' first‑hand quotes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories include explicit attribution to individuals and quoted speech to convey authority and immediacy. Example quotes: officials' criticisms and defenses in Congressional debate; survivors' first‑hand reports of sinking and rescue; operational statements by military officers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include official responses and competing perspectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Present official denials, clarifications or counterstatements alongside accusations or claims (e.g., OWI denial of circulating 'fourth-term propaganda', replies from Elmer Davis; Congressional debate and rebuttals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When allegations or criticisms appear (propaganda charges, preferential treatment claims), the article presents official denials or alternative viewpoints, enabling readers to see multiple sides of the issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human-interest and biographical detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Embed personal, family and biographical details to humanize wartime stories (e.g., profiles of Roosevelt's sons, survivors' family information, biographical notes on officers and casualties).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Articles supply background (education, assignments, illnesses, promotions, family survivors) and anecdotes to create emotional and narrative interest beyond raw facts. Examples include descriptions of illnesses, hospital operations, promotions, and family details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical and tactical specifics for military reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide operational details and quantitative facts about military events (e.g., 'vessel plunged to the bottom 25 minutes after a single, powerful torpedo', casualties numbers, types of aircraft and tactics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good wartime reporting includes times, numbers, weapon and platform types, tactical descriptions (raiding methods, aircraft performance), and outcomes (loss counts, rescue details) to give readers concrete sense of events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of clear headlines and subheads to separate stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinct headlines and subheads are used to delineate different items on the page (e.g., 'Lifeboats Should Carry, Guns, Fishing Gear, Navy Doctor Says', 'End of Attacks on His Brothers', '4th Term Plea to Army').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Headlines concisely summarize main point; subheads or bolded lines help readers scan the front page for items of interest and follow multiple concurrent stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual background and linkage to broader issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories situate events within larger political, diplomatic or military contexts (e.g., debate over a fourth term for the President, propaganda distribution overseas, allied relations with Britain and the Soviet Union, plans for expeditionary forces).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reports include surrounding context and prior developments so readers understand significance and implications beyond the immediate incident; e.g., references to prior debates, allied strategy and public sentiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: First‑person eyewitness accounts for dramatic scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: Inclusion of survivors' vivid first‑person recollections to convey the drama of an event (e.g., descriptions of ship sinking, 'the last I saw of our ship, she was on her side with her mast to the water', swimming to lifeboats).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eyewitness testimony is used to reconstruct events and give immediacy; such accounts are presented alongside official statistics and expert commentary to balance narrative color with verification.
